**Ill-conditioning means different directions operate on very different scales.** In a positive-definite quadratic loss, large Hessian eigenvalues correspond to steep directions and small ones to flat directions. One global learning rate must avoid overshooting the steep direction while still making progress along the flat one. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

**Picture a long narrow valley.** The gradient points strongly across the valley because that curvature is steep, even though the desired progress is mostly along it. A large step bounces across; a safe small step makes slow forward progress. This produces the familiar zig-zag trajectory.

For a positive-definite Hessian, the eigenvalue ratio describes this disparity. More generally, the 2-norm matrix condition number uses singular values. An indefinite Hessian has negative curvature and needs a different interpretation from a simple convex bowl.

Feature standardization can reduce avoidable scale differences; preconditioning and adaptive methods change the effective coordinate system; momentum can reduce oscillation. None is a guarantee that every nonlinear landscape becomes well-conditioned.

A zero singular value makes the matrix condition number infinite, but a flat parameter direction can reflect symmetry or nonidentifiability rather than a failure to predict. Distinguish solving for a unique parameter vector from obtaining useful predictions, and use stable solvers instead of explicit inverses when analyzing related linear systems.

**Technical details and references.**

For a positive-definite quadratic with Hessian $H$, different eigenvalues determine curvature along different directions. A step stable in the steepest direction may be tiny relative to what the flattest direction needs. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

$$\kappa(H)=\lambda_{max}/\lambda_{min},\qquad 0<\eta<2/\lambda_{max}.$$

This causes slow progress and oscillation across a narrow valley. For a general matrix, the 2-norm condition number is the singular-value ratio; an indefinite Hessian needs additional care because negative curvature invalidates the simple convex convergence picture. Standardization, preconditioning, momentum, and adaptive methods can improve effective geometry. A singular Hessian has infinite condition number under this definition, though the optimization problem may still have useful flat directions rather than a unique minimizer.
